profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting at a fintech research company preparing the public release of a cross-bank NLP benchmark based on central bank communications. The team has already completed the paper draft and internal benchmarking, and this meeting is to align the research workstream and the partnerships/compliance workstream before a conference submission deadline and a companion artifact release. The context is that the company wants to publish a polished 'release package' for the World Central Banks framework, including the dataset card, benchmark tables, repository structure, and external access instructions. The agenda is to confirm what goes into the release package, which benchmark results are considered the current baseline, how the dataset version should be handed off for publication, and who owns the external-facing access materials. The expected outcome is apparent agreement on a Friday handoff, a shared understanding that the benchmark package is ready, and a plan for posting the artifacts after legal review—while subtle misalignments remain unresolved.

members.name: Leah Morgan
members.expertise: Coordinating ML research deliverables, experiment tracking, paper submission packaging, and cross-team handoffs
members.background: Leah has spent six years managing NLP research launches in financial services firms and is known for keeping publication timelines on track across modeling, annotation, and documentation teams.
members.private_state: She wants the research package frozen quickly so the paper and artifact appendix stay consistent, and she is trying to avoid any late-cycle reopening of benchmark runs or dataset edits that could delay submission.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'the benchmark package,' they mean the conference-facing artifact bundle tied to the paper draft, not a broader public distribution set.
The 'current version' is the frozen research snapshot from the internal experiment registry created after the final model sweep last week.
A deliverable is 'ready' once the required files exist, naming is stable, and the package can be reproduced internally without additional narrative polish.
Publishing access instructions is a communications task that sits with partnerships/compliance once research hands over the technical artifacts.

members.name: Daniel Cho
members.expertise: External data release processes, licensing interpretation, repository governance, documentation standards, and public artifact launch coordination
members.background: Daniel previously managed open-data releases for a market intelligence firm and now oversees how research outputs are packaged for external users, including licensing notices, access flows, and public-facing documentation.
members.private_state: He wants to ensure the release is externally usable and low-risk, and he is concerned that research teams often treat internal reproducibility as equivalent to public release readiness.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'the benchmark package,' they mean the full public release bundle: dataset card, license notices, usage constraints, model-result summary, and access instructions.
The 'current version' is the cleaned export prepared for external release after redaction checks, even if it lags the latest internal experiment snapshot.
A deliverable is only 'ready' if an outside user can understand, access, and use it without asking the research team follow-up questions.
Because the artifacts are going to HuggingFace and GitHub, the research team should provide the first draft of the external-facing access and usage documentation.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the benchmark package
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss finalizing 'the benchmark package' for Friday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the research artifact bundle: benchmark tables, scripts, model configs, and the dataset snapshot referenced in the paper appendix.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the public release package: the research artifact bundle plus dataset card, license text, access instructions, and user-facing repository structure.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In research-release settings, 'benchmark package' sounds naturally shared, and both scopes overlap enough that each speaker hears confirmation of their own broader or narrower interpretation.

misalignment_points.topic: Which version is the current release candidate
misalignment_points.surface_form: They refer to using 'the current version' and 'the latest snapshot' in the handoff.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the internal experiment snapshot frozen after the final 15,075-run benchmark sweep, stored in the experiment registry and matching the paper tables.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the externally cleaned export assembled after legal and redaction checks for publication staging, stored in the release folder.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both versions are recent, both are called 'latest' within their own workstreams, and neither participant expects that the other would be indexing a different storage location for something presented as the same release candidate.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree that the package should be 'ready for release' before legal sign-off.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes 'ready for release' means technically complete and internally reproducible, with only formal approval remaining.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes 'ready for release' means understandable and usable by external researchers, including sufficient explanatory documentation and access guidance.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both criteria are common and professionally legitimate, so the phrase sounds like routine alignment rather than a term needing unpacking.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss posting the access instructions once the package is finalized.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes Daniel's team will draft and own the access instructions because they manage external release operations.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes Leah's team will provide the first draft because research knows the artifact contents and intended usage best.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Each sees their assumption as standard operating procedure, so the conversation can smoothly reference 'the access instructions' without either side noticing that authorship has never been explicitly assigned.

turns.inner_thought: I need this frozen now. The benchmark package, as far as I’m concerned, is the conference artifact bundle tied to the paper: tables, scripts, configs, and the exact dataset snapshot from last week’s final sweep. If we let that expand into a broader release discussion, we risk reopening files and shifting appendix references right before submission.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I want to lock the benchmark package this week so the paper appendix, the repo contents, and the Friday handoff all stay aligned.

turns.inner_thought: That timing works if Friday means we’re finalizing the full public release bundle. For me the benchmark package includes the external-facing pieces too, and I want it stable enough that I can keep the posting queue moving without a last-minute scramble on documentation or repository setup.
turns.utterance: That works from my side. Once the benchmark package is finalized, I can move the public posting queue forward.

turns.inner_thought: I’m talking about the internal experiment registry snapshot from the final 15,075-run sweep. That’s the current version that matches the paper tables. I need to hand off that exact snapshot so no one swaps in anything cleaner or newer and accidentally breaks consistency with the draft.
turns.utterance: My proposal is that we hand over the current version from the final experiment sweep so nothing shifts under the reported benchmark tables.

turns.inner_thought: Good, we should stay on the cleaned export in the release folder. That’s the latest snapshot I’ve already been checking for redaction and licensing. It may not be the exact research registry state, but it’s the one that’s actually viable for publication staging.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I’ve already been reviewing the latest snapshot in the release folder for licensing and staging, so that should fit cleanly into the handoff.

turns.inner_thought: From my standpoint, ready for release means the technical package is complete: runs are done, configs are stable, files are named, and the dataset snapshot reproduces internally. I do not want this turning into a request for more editorial work before we can call it ready.
turns.utterance: I think the package should be ready for release by Friday, since the runs, configs, and dataset files are all stable now.

turns.inner_thought: Friday is fine if ready for release means an external user can actually make sense of it. I still need the benchmark package to include the public-facing context—dataset card, usage framing, and enough structure that outside researchers won’t have to email us basic questions.
turns.utterance: Friday works for me as long as the package is ready for release with the dataset card, the usage framing, and enough context for outside researchers to navigate it.

turns.inner_thought: I can make sure the research-facing materials are in place and the repo is orderly. Access instructions are really Daniel’s lane once the technical artifacts are finalized; partnerships and compliance always handle that external communications layer after handoff.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I’ll make sure the benchmark tables and repository structure are in place, and the access instructions can go out alongside the rest once the package is finalized.

turns.inner_thought: Great, so research is planning to provide the first draft of the access instructions. I mainly need them to line up with approved license language and explain how people actually obtain the artifacts, then my team can review and post.
turns.utterance: Great. As long as the access instructions reflect the approved license language and explain how users should obtain the artifacts, that should be in good shape.

turns.inner_thought: I want to state this clearly without inviting debate: the current version is the frozen research snapshot, and I do not want any newer files substituted after handoff. The benchmark numbers are already locked for the paper, and any late swap creates risk for submission consistency.
turns.utterance: The other thing I want to hold on is the current version. I’d really like to avoid swapping in anything newer after the handoff, because the benchmark numbers are already frozen.

turns.inner_thought: I’m not planning big content changes to the cleaned release candidate, but I do need it complete enough for legal that they’re mostly confirming rather than discovering gaps. Ready for release should mean we’re close to publishable, not just technically assembled.
turns.utterance: I’m not expecting substantive changes. I just want the release candidate to be complete enough that legal review is mostly a formality.

turns.inner_thought: Good. Then the plan is straightforward: research hands over the benchmark package Friday, and Daniel’s team takes it through the external posting steps, including the access materials. I just need the package freeze respected so the paper and artifact appendix remain synchronized.
turns.utterance: Perfect. So by Friday, research will hand over the benchmark package, and then partnerships can take it through the posting process.

turns.inner_thought: Sounds good. I’ll keep working from the latest release materials I already have, expect the Friday package to fill in the remaining public-facing pieces, and assume the access instructions will come over with it so we can line everything up for publication after sign-off.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I’ll watch for the Friday package, continue with the latest release materials, and line things up for publication after sign-off.
